title: Phase-controlled molecular beam deposition unlocks flexible MgAgSb thermoelectrics with exceptional performance

paper_content.abstract: Flexible thermoelectric materials hold great promise for sustainable energy supply in flexible electronics. However, beyond the long-standing champion Bi2Te3-based flexible films, high-performance alternatives remain scarce. Here, we report a promising flexible thermoelectric material based on eco-friendly MgAgSb, a bulk-proven high-performance system whose development in flexible form has long been hindered by its intrinsic brittleness and phase complexity. Using molecular beam deposition, we manage to precisely stabilize MgAgSb within its α-phase range and finely control its stoichiometry. As a result, we successfully fabricate the α-MgAgSb film with exceptional performance, achieving a room temperature zT of 0.8 and a peak power factor of 19.3 μW cm-1 K-2, ranking among the promising flexible thermoelectric materials developed. Moreover, the α-MgAgSb film is revealed to exhibit notable flexibility and stability under repeated bending and heating. Leveraging this high-performance stable α-MgAgSb film, the flexible thermoelectric device delivers a maximum normalized power density of 4.9 μW cm-2 K-2. This work opens a pathway for flexible MgAgSb applications and offers strong potential for realizing self-powered flexible technologies.
paper_content.introduction:
Flexible electronics are emerging technologies that enable advancements in wearable devices, healthcare monitoring, and soft robotics, while also opening new possibilities for applications in high-temperature environments above 373K, such as aerospace surface monitoring and engine diagnostics1. However, continuously and maintenance-free powering of electronic components within flexible devices remains a critical challenge2. Thermoelectric (TE) devices, which can directly harvest heat from surfaces and the environment to generate sustainable electrical energy, offer a promising alternative to traditional batteries3–5. Typically, TE devices consist of n-type and p-type TE materials connected in series to convert heat into electricity, and their conversion efficiency is fundamentally determined by the dimensionless figure of merit (zT) of the constituent TE materials6. zT is defined as zT = S2σT/κ = PF × T/κ, where S is the Seebeck coefficient, σ is the electrical conductivity, κ is the total thermal conductivity, PF (= S2σ) is the power factor, a metric of electrical performance. It means that achieving high zT requires materials with both a high PF and a low κ. Beyond high TE performance, in the context of flexible thermoelectrics, the mechanical flexibility of TE materials and devices is also a key prerequisite7,8.

However, flexibility and TE performance are two different material attributes. Achieving both high flexibility and high TE performance in a single material remains highly challenging, making suitable candidates for flexible thermoelectrics extremely scarce9. Organic thermoelectric (TE) materials offer excellent flexibility due to their molecular and polymeric structures, but suffer from low electrical performance10. Although significant efforts have been devoted to enhancing systems such as PEDOT: PSS11–13, PANI14, SWCNT15,16, and PMHJ17, their zT and PF values remain far below those of inorganic TE materials. Hybridizing organics with inorganics can provide moderate performance and flexibility, but weak interfacial bonding and still-inferior TE properties hinder practical use18,19. To date, inorganic TE compounds remain the leaders in TE performance, with materials such as SnSe and GeTe achieving zT values exceeding 220–24. However, their brittleness limits flexible applications.

Reducing the dimensional size of materials to the micro- or nanoscale is an effective approach to endow brittle materials with flexibility through either top-down or bottom-up methods9,25–27. Top-down processing is often limited by their intrinsic brittleness. Only a few inorganic compounds, including Ag2(S, Se, Te)9,26,28, Mg3(Sb, Bi)229, single-crystalline Bi2Te330 and some van der Waals compounds31 exhibit intrinsic plasticity that enables safer deformation and flexible device fabrication32–34. In most cases, bottom-up synthesis of thin films (e.g., by printing or various deposition) is preferred, offering flexibility and tunability35,36. Currently, research on thin-film-based flexible inorganic TE materials has mainly focused on Bi2Te337–39 and Ag2Se40–42 due to their superior room temperature TE performance. For instance, p-type Bi0.3Sb1.7Te3 can achieve a zT value exceeding 1 at room temperature43, while n-type Ag2Se exhibits a comparable performance under similar conditions40. However, their performance deteriorates rapidly at elevated temperatures, posing an obstacle for their applications in flexible devices operating above 373K. Furthermore, the toxicity of Te/Se and the scarcity of Te impose additional limitations on their practical deployment44.

In contrast, α-MgAgSb is an eco-friendly and high-performance TE material, exhibiting zT values of ~0.8 at room temperature and peak values of around 1.3 above 473K45. Its intrinsically high PF across the working temperature range stems from its high band degeneracy, while its complex crystal structure results in its intrinsically low lattice thermal conductivity46,47. These merits make α-MgAgSb one of the most promising p-type TE materials near room temperature, particularly as a potential substitute for p-type (Bi, Sb)2Te3 in power generation. However, the TE performance of α-MgAgSb is highly sensitive to impurities such as Ag3Sb48, and α-MgAgSb will also undergo phase transitions to β- and γ-MgAgSb at elevated temperatures, complicating the fabrication of high-performance α-MgAgSb. Many processing optimizations have been reported to improve the phase purity and reliability of bulk α-MgAgSb, advancing its use in rigid TE devices45,49.

Despite these encouraging developments, studies on α-MgAgSb have so far been limited to rigid bulk forms, leaving its application in flexible thermoelectrics largely unexplored.

α-MgAgSb is intrinsically brittle, making it particularly difficult to impart flexibility through top-down processing methods. A more promising route is to fabricate α-MgAgSb thin films via bottom-up approaches. However, the complex phase behavior of MgAgSb poses significant challenges for film fabrication, and achieving flexible α-MgAgSb films with high performance remains elusive. In previous work, Wang et al.50 prepared flexible MgAgSb-based films by solution-casting mixtures of α-MgAgSb powder with graphene and PEDOT:PSS. However, the presence of multiple phases and interfaces in such inorganic/organic composites led to TE performance far below that of bulk α-MgAgSb. Besides, Oueldna et al. attempted to co-deposit Mg, Ag and Sb using magnetron sputtering. However, regardless of how the initial composition ratio was adjusted, the resulting films failed to form pure α-MgAgSb as the main phase51,52. At present, despite the promising TE potential of α-MgAgSb, a phase-pure and high-performance α-MgAgSb film suitable for flexible TE devices has not yet been realized.

In this work, we employ molecular beam deposition to precisely stabilize MgAgSb within its α-phase range and finely tune its stoichiometry. This deposition technique provides a quasi-equilibrium growth environment that favors the formation of phase-pure α-MgAgSb while suppressing secondary phases. Consequently, we successfully obtain the flexible inorganic α-MgAgSb thin film with exceptional TE performance, achieving a zT value of 0.8 at room temperature and a peak PF of 19.3 μW cm−1 K-2 at 473K, placing these films among the promising flexible p-type TE candidates beyond Bi2Te3. Using this technique, we further investigate the impact of stoichiometric deviations and find that slight deficiencies in composition degrade the TE performance of α-MgAgSb. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the fabricated α-MgAgSb film exhibits notable flexibility and thermal stability, maintains performance after 1000 bending cycles and repeated thermal cycling between 373K and 473K. Finally, we fabricate a flexible thermoelectric device based on these films, realizing an estimated normalized power density of 4.9 μW cm-2 K-2, suggesting their strong practical potential. This work marks an important step in the exploration of flexible α-MgAgSb and provides valuable insights for integrating MgAgSb-based thermoelectrics in flexible electronics.
paper_content.results:
High-performance flexible α-MgAgSb film
MgAgSb exhibits three polymorphs over different temperature ranges: α-MgAgSb, β-MgAgSb, and γ-MgAgSb. Among them, only α-MgAgSb shows high TE potential with large zT values, whereas both β- and γ-MgAgSb display poor performance. A recent study has demonstrated that β-MgAgSb can be strategically utilized in α/β-segmented junctions to enhance power output while maintaining conversion efficiency53. However, the formation of β- or especially γ-MgAgSb within the MgAgSb matrix will degrade its overall TE performance. As shown in Fig. 1a, γ-MgAgSb forms from β-MgAgSb upon heating, accompanied by the precipitation of Ag3Sb and Sb. Once γ-MgAgSb, Ag3Sb, and Sb appear, they remain even after cooling to room temperature, which not only deteriorates MgAgSb performance but also complicates the synthesis of high-quality MgAgSb. This issue is particularly critical for film fabrication. Magnetron sputtering, a commonly used deposition technique, has consistently failed to produce high-performance α-MgAgSb films because of extensive impurity formation. Typically, during sputtering, energetic atoms, ions, and excited species with high kinetic energies and fluctuating fluxes lead to non-uniform nucleation and far-from-equilibrium growth, making the formation of secondary phases easy. These problems are particularly severe for MgAgSb due to the above-mentioned complex phase behavior. In addition, the high vapor pressure and reactivity of Mg under the relatively low vacuum of the sputtering chamber result in Mg loss and undesired reactions during deposition, which further disturb the stoichiometry and hinder precise phase control, making it difficult to fabricate high-performance MgAgSb films.

To achieve a high-performance α-MgAgSb film, precise phase control during deposition is essential. First, the reaction temperature must be strictly maintained below 573K to keep MgAgSb within the α-phase stability range. Second, the deposited Mg, Ag and Sb atoms need to thoroughly react under near-equilibrium conditions. Third, a high-vacuum environment is required to prevent oxidation and undesirable reactions of Mg. Based on these requirements, we employed molecular beam deposition (Fig. 1b), which offers ideal growth conditions for the MgAgSb film. In this process, low-energy neutral Mg, Ag and Sb atoms arrive at the substrate in well-collimated molecular beams under ultra-high vacuum. The slow and gentle deposition enables controlled surface diffusion and reaction of these atoms under quasi-equilibrium conditions, forming α-MgAgSb when the substrate temperature is maintained at 523K. It is worth noting that although a molecular beam epitaxy system was used, the substrate was a flexible polyimide rather than a conventional single-crystalline substrate, which enables both film growth and mechanical flexibility. Supplementary Fig. S1 shows the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the molecular-beam-deposited films, which match well with the corresponding powder diffraction patterns of the α-MgAgSb phase, confirming that flexible α-MgAgSb films were successfully obtained on polyimide substrates (Fig. 1c).

Importantly, as shown in Fig. 1d, the flexible MgAgSb films exhibit an excellent room-temperature zT of 0.8. Although this value is slightly lower than that of state-of-the-art p-type Bi2Te3-based flexible materials, it is significantly higher than those of other reported flexible TE films. Moreover, as shown in Fig. 1e, the α-MgAgSb film shows an increasing PF, reaching a maximum of 19.3 μW cm−1 K−2 at 473K. This temperature-dependent enhancement leads to a high average power factor (PFavg) of 17.2 μW cm−1 K−2 over the range of 293–523K (Fig. 1f). The exceptional performance (zT and PF) of α-MgAgSb in this work can be attributed to the successful synthesis of high-purity α-MgAgSb. Intrinsically, the favorable band structure of high band degeneracy, as well as large anharmonicity and weak chemical bonding in α-MgAgSb, enables its high PF and zT compared to other materials. These results highlight the strong potential of flexible α-MgAgSb films for TE applications even beyond room temperature.

Elemental deficiency effects on TE performance
MgAgSb is known to be highly sensitive to stoichiometry54. Molecular beam deposition provides an ideal platform to investigate how stoichiometric deviation affects the TE performance of flexible MgAgSb film. By carefully adjusting the flux rate of Mg, Ag and Sb (Supplementary Fig. S2 and Supplementary Table S1), we intentionally introduced a 5% deficiency in each element to allow a clearer observation of the effects of non-stoichiometry on the TE properties of MgAgSb thin films, producing Mg-deficient, Ag-deficient, and Sb-deficient films, respectively. XRD patterns confirmed that all these films remain primarily in the α-MgAgSb phase (Supplementary Fig. S3). The TE performance of these films was systematically measured over a temperature range of 303K to 523K to assess the impact of these deficiencies, with the corresponding thickness data shown in Supplementary Fig. S4. As shown in Fig. 2a, Sb and Ag deficiencies lead to higher resistivity ρ of the films, whereas Mg deficiency decreases ρ. Figure 2b shows the S of these films, and the S increases in the Sb-deficient, slightly decreases in Ag-deficient films, and drops markedly in the Mg-deficient film. Consequently, all deficient films exhibit lower PF than the stoichiometric film (Fig. 2c), underscoring the critical role of precise phase and composition control in achieving high-performance α-MgAgSb films.

To further elucidate the impact of elemental deficiencies on charge transport, we measured the Hall carrier concentration nH and mobility μH of each α-MgAgSb film at room temperature. As shown in Fig. 2d, the stoichiometric film exhibits an nH of 3.9 × 1019 cm−3 and a μH of 53 cm2 V−1 s−1, values consistent with those reported for high-performance bulk α-MgAgSb55. For the element-deficient films, Sb deficiency is observed to reduce the room-temperature nH, which may arise from the formation of Sb vacancies (V3+Sb). These vacancies act as electron donors, leading to a decreased nH and consequently an increased S according to the Pisarenko relation. In the case of Ag deficiency, Ag vacancies (V−Ag) may be induced, increasing nH, as reflected by the decreasing trend of S over a broad temperature range. In contrast, Mg deficiency markedly increases nH due to the formation of Mg vacancies (V2−Mg) and Ag-Mg antistites defects (AgMg)56,57, resulting in a much lower S. Notably, μH decreases uniformly in all deficient films, primarily due to enhanced carrier scattering from point defects and possible secondary phases associated with non-stoichiometry. The reduced μH intrinsically deteriorates electrical transport, resulting in all deficient films exhibiting lower PFs than the non-deficient sample. Since charge transport is also strongly influenced by the electronic band structure, we further investigated how elemental deficiencies modify the band structure of α-MgAgSb. As shown in Fig. 2e, Ag and Mg deficiencies exert little influence on the valence band maximum (VBM) between the X and Γ points, whereas Sb deficiency significantly distorts the VBM. This distortion likely explains the pronounced reduction in mobility observed in Sb-deficient films. Overall, among the various elemental deficiencies, Sb deficiency is the most detrimental, leading to both the lowest carrier nH and μH, and thus causing the greatest degradation in electrical performance, with the PF of the Sb-deficient film being only half that of the non-deficient film.

In addition to electrical performance, the cross-plane thermal conductivity κ of these films was measured at room temperature using the time-domain thermoreflectance method and is presented in Supplementary Figs. S5, S6 and Supplementary Table S2. All films exhibit lower κ compared to reported bulk values. The non-deficient MgAgSb film shows a κ of 0.61 W m−1 K−1, while the deficient films show even lower values. Benefiting from the ultralow κ and relatively high PF, the non-deficient flexible MgAgSb film achieves a room-temperature zT of approximately 0.8, which is comparable to that of state-of-the-art MgAgSb bulk. However, despite the lower κ values in element-deficient films, all of them exhibit reduced zT values. In particular, the zT of the Sb-deficient film drops to around 0.5 at room temperature (Supplementary Fig. S7), primarily due to its pronounced decline in PF.

Microstructure, stability and flexibility of α-MgAgSb film
MgAgSb is intrinsically a low κ system. The α-MgAgSb films fabricated by molecular beam deposition exhibit lower κ than most conventional bulk α-MgAgSb, as noted in the previous section55. To elucidate the origin of their low κ, we examined the microstructures of stoichiometric and element-deficient films using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). As shown in Fig. 3a and Supplementary Figs. S8, S9, the stoichiometric, Ag‑deficient, and Mg‑deficient films display uniform and compact surfaces, whereas the Sb‑deficient film shows poor and uneven crystal quality, indicating that Sb deficiency is unfavorable for the growth of α-MgAgSb crystals. Notably, the grains in all films are nanosized; for example, the stoichiometric film has grain sizes of about 60-90 nm, as displayed in Fig. 3b. The nanoscale grain structure reveals the polycrystalline nature of the films. Together with the absence of obvious preferred orientation in the XRD patterns (Supplementary Fig S1), the films are therefore expected to exhibit nearly isotropic TE properties, even though S and σ were measured in-plane, while κ was measured cross-plane. These nanoscale grains result from the low deposition temperature, which limits atomic diffusion and grain growth. To further investigate compositional uniformity, we also applied the energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis. As shown in Fig. 3c and Supplementary Figs. S10–S12, Mg, Ag and Sb are homogeneously distributed in the stoichiometric, Ag-deficient, and Mg-deficient films. In contrast, the Sb-deficient film contains Mg-rich regions (Supplementary Fig. S12), evidencing impurity formation.

To gain deeper insight into the impact of elemental deficiencies on thermal transport, we have decomposed the total thermal conductivity into its electronic and lattice components (Supplementary Note S1 and Supplementary Fig. S13). It is evident that Sb deficiency leads to an increase in lattice thermal conductivity (κL), whereas Mg deficiency results in a pronounced reduction in κL. In comparison, Ag deficiency has a relatively minor influence on κL. The increased κL observed in Sb-deficient films likely originates from the formation of Mg-rich metallic secondary phases, as evidenced in Supplementary Figs. S9 and S12. In contrast, the presence of Mg vacancies and Ag-Mg antisite defects in Mg-deficient films enhances phonon scattering, thereby reducing κL48. Notably, although all these films exhibit a reduced κL compared with bulk samples due to enhanced phonon scattering from nanoscale grains, such nanoscale grains can also induce carrier scattering, leading to a relatively lower carrier mobility than that of bulk counterparts49 and consequently relatively low zT values.

Overall, stoichiometric films exhibit the best TE performance among α-MgAgSb thin films, and even slight Sb deficiency should be avoided whenever possible. In addition to high performance of the stoichiometric films, thermal stability and mechanical stability are essential for their practical applications in flexible electronics38. We first evaluated the thermal stability of the film under repeated measurements at 373K and 473K (the temperature of peak PF). As shown in Fig. 3d, the electrical transport properties, including the S, σ, and PF, remain unchanged, demonstrating excellent thermal stability under elevated-temperature operation. This stability can be attributed to the intrinsic phase stability of α-MgAgSb, which is thermodynamically stable over a broad temperature range and does not undergo phase transitions or decomposition within the temperature window investigated in this work58. We then assessed the flexibility of the α-MgAgSb film by subjecting it to repeated bending at a fixed bending radius of 10 mm, corresponding to an applied strain of approximately 0.75% (Supplementary Note S2 and Fig. 3e). The ratios of S/S0, σ/σ0, and PF/PF0 (where S0, σ0, and PF0 are the initial values) are found to remain nearly constant with increasing bending cycles. Remarkably, after 1000 bending cycles, the PF of the film retains 96% of its initial value within a 5% measurement error. The surface morphology after 1000 bending cycles (Supplementary Fig. S14) shows few cracks. These results confirm the excellent flexibility and durability of the α-MgAgSb film. This high flexibility arises from the small film thickness (about 180 nm), which allows large elastic bending strains25, together with the intrinsically flexible polyimide substrate that redistributes bending-induced stress and reduces the effective strain in the film. Consequently, the α-MgAgSb films show strong potential for flexible TE power generation under practical operating conditions, including applications requiring mechanical compliance and thermal robustness.

High-performance flexible α-MgAgSb TE device
To evaluate the practical potential of the flexible α-MgAgSb film, we fabricated a flexible TE device consisting of nine MgAgSb legs electrically connected in series using Ag interconnects (Fig. 4a). For power generation, one side of the flexible TE device is heated, enabling in-plane heat flow. Based on this configuration, we measured the open-circuit voltage (Voc) generated by the TE device and the output power under different hot-side temperatures with varying loading current (I). As shown in Fig. 4b, when the hot-side temperature is 393K (estimated ΔT=16K), the Voc reaches 40 mV. As the hot-side temperature increases to 513K (estimated ΔT=40K), the Voc rises to 66 mV. The relationship between Voc and ΔT is shown in Supplementary Fig. S15, clearly demonstrating that Voc of TE device increases with ΔT. Based on the measured output voltage and current, the output power was calculated. The maximum output power (Pmax) is achieved when the internal resistance of the device matches the external load resistance, as shown in Supplementary Fig. S16. Consequently, a normalized power density (Pmax/AΔT2) of 4.9 μW cm−2 K−2 is obtained at a hot-side temperature of 513K. As shown in Fig. 4c and Supplementary Table S3, the normalized power density achieved in this work ranks among the leading values ever reported for flexible in-plane TE devices based on other material systems, highlighting the excellent potential of α-MgAgSb for flexible energy conversion applications. Notably, the device operates reliably at elevated temperatures up to 513K, making it suitable not only for wearable electronics but also for practical applications such as aerospace surface monitoring, engine diagnostics, and smart factories, where moderate temperature gradients are available.

To further reveal the flexibility of the device, we measured the output voltage and output power under bending conditions, as shown in Supplementary Fig. S17. At a hot stage temperature of 513K, the Voc is 58 mV, and the Pmax reaches 0.36 μW. It should be noted that the flexible TE device was mounted on the curved surface of a carbon pillar rather than directly on a flat heating stage, resulting in a different effective hot-side temperature on the device and, consequently, variations in the measured output voltage and power. In addition to testing under curved-surface conditions, we further evaluated the mechanical flexibility of the flexible MgAgSb TE device through repeated bending tests. Unlike a single TE film, a TE device includes additional electrical contacts, making such tests essential. As shown in Fig. 4d, after 1000 bending cycles with a fixed bending radius of 10 mm, the device’s internal resistance R increased only slightly by about 6% compared to its initial internal resistance R0. Meanwhile, the Pmax/A after 1000 bending cycles remained almost unchanged compared to its initial value (Fig. 4e). These results demonstrate the excellent flexibility and reliability of the device for potential practical flexible TE applications. To further illustrate its potential, we tested the device under finger-induced temperature gradients. As shown in Fig. 4f, g, the device generated an output voltage of about 3.0 mV and a maximum output power of 0.88 nW when placed on the side or tip of a finger, highlighting its promise for wearable technology and paving the way for flexible TE devices as sustainable power sources for flexible electronics59.

In summary, by succeeding to precisely stabilizing MgAgSb within its α-phase range and finely controlling its composition using advanced molecular beam deposition, we have successfully fabricated high-performance flexible α-MgAgSb films. This flexible α-MgAgSb film achieves a zT value of 0.8 at room temperature and a PF of 19.3 μW cm−1 K−2 at 473K, surpassing most flexible TE materials and second only to the long-standing champion, flexible Bi2Te3 films. Notably, the PF of flexible α-MgAgSb film increases with temperature, leading to an excellent average PF of 17.2 μW cm−1 K−2 in the 293–523K range. This measured increase in PF with temperature, together with the expected decrease in thermal conductivity at elevated temperatures due to enhanced phonon scattering, suggests that zT values exceeding 0.8 may be achievable at higher temperatures. Beyond its high performance, the flexible α-MgAgSb film shows remarkable thermal stability and mechanical flexibility under thermal and bending cycles. Finally, a flexible TE device comprising nine α-MgAgSb film legs is demonstrated to exhibit an estimated normalized power density of 4.9 μW cm−2 K−2, demonstrating strong potential for power generation in flexible electronics. In future studies, strategies such as grain enlargement and doping could be explored to further enhance TE performance, as the current films still underperform compared with optimized bulk materials. Moreover, developing scalable, large-area fabrication routes and integrating these films into flexible device architectures will be crucial for more practical applications. Nevertheless, this work opens a new pathway for flexible applications of α-MgAgSb and represents an important step toward self-powered flexible technologies.
paper_content.methods:
Film fabrication
All flexible α-MgAgSb films were deposited on a polyimide substrate using a molecular beam epitaxy system (EV-500, Eiko). The base pressure in the chamber was 10⁻⁸ Pa, and the working pressure was maintained in the 10-7 Pa range during deposition. Mg, Ag, and Sb of 4N purity were placed in separate Knudsen cells and heated to the specified temperatures. The evaporation rate of each element was determined using a retractable quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) thickness monitor (Q-pod, Inficon), located at the substrate position. The substrate was heated from the back of the sample stage. A thermocouple measured the temperature between the sample holder and the heater, which controlled the heater power to keep a specified temperature. The actual substrate temperature was consistent with the set temperature when the temperature was below 773K. The polyimide substrate was immersed in acetone and subjected to ultrasonic cleaning for 30 minutes to remove surface organic contaminants and dust before being transferred into the vacuum chamber. It was heated to 523K and held for 30 minutes to remove residual impurities before deposition. The α-MgAgSb films were prepared by co-depositing Mg, Ag, and Sb with a 1:1:1 flux ratio, monitored by a QCM, at a substrate temperature of 523K. Compositional analysis was performed by EDS on films deposited on Al2O3 substrate under the same conditions as those on polyimide. As shown in Supplementary Fig. S18 and Supplementary Table S4, the film composition closely matches the intended 1:1:1 ratio. Based on this result, off-stoichiometric films were fabricated by individually reducing the flux of each element by 5% during deposition. EDS analysis further confirms a ~5% Sb deficiency in the corresponding film (Supplementary Fig. S18 and Supplementary Table S4). The films were deposited at a rate of 6 nm per minute for 30 min with the substrate rotating at 5 rpm, resulting in a thickness of approximately 180 nm.

Characterization
The phase composition and crystallinity of the stoichiometric MgAgSb film were examined using XRD and grazing incidence XRD (GIXRD). XRD measurements were performed on a Rigaku MiniFlex diffractometer with a Cu Kα+β source, while GIXRD was carried out using a Rigaku TF-XRD system equipped with a Cu Kα source. Both techniques reveal the characteristic diffraction peaks of the α-MgAgSb phase. Because GIXRD measurements are more time-consuming, conventional XRD, which provides reliable and efficient phase identification, was used for all element-deficient films. The surface morphology of films was analyzed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Hitachi High-Tech/S-4800), and the component was analyzed using energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) (Hitachi High-Tech/TM-3000). The film thicknesses were measured using a surface profiler system (Bruker Dektak 6M) by the step method. The step was created from an uncovered area of the substrate to the film surface. The measurement uncertainty was within 10 nm. Hall carrier concentration and mobility at 300K were measured using a four-probe Hall system (Biorad H5580) under a magnetic field of 0.45 T using the van der Pauw method, which is suitable for samples of arbitrary geometry. The probes were placed at the corners of the film, and the insulating substrate did not affect the measurements. Multiple measurements were performed to ensure stable contacts, with an uncertainty of approximately 1%. The electric conductivity and Seebeck coefficient of thin films were measured using a ZEM-3 (Advance Riko) apparatus in a He atmosphere, with samples having lateral dimensions of 10 mm × 3 mm. Multiple measurements confirmed good reproducibility of the film fabrication, with variations within approximately 5% (Supplementary Fig. S19). The cross-plane thermal conductivity of the samples was measured using the picosecond time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) instrument (PicoTR, PicoTherm) in a front-heating/front-detection configuration. Prior to the measurements, a ~100 nm-thick Pt layer was sputtered onto the thin-film surfaces by using a DC sputtering system to serve as a transducer. A 1550 nm infrared pulsed laser with a repetition frequency of 20 MHz and a pulse duration of 0.5 ps was used as a heat source. A 780 nm probe laser was used to detect the thermoreflectance signal. The picosecond TDTR system was customized to reduce the spot size of the probe laser to ca. 5 μm as described elsewhere60. The improved mirror image method for fitting all the range of pulse interval was used to determine the thermal conductivity value61,62. In Supplementary Fig. S5, the measured thermoreflectance signals are shown together with the fitted curves. The interfacial thermal resistance (ITR) between the MgAgSb film and the Pt layer is extracted to be smaller than 1.0 × 10-8 m2 KW-1 for all films (Supplementary Table S2), indicating that the possible error introduced in film thermal conductivity is at most about 3%. The specific heat of all films was calculated based on the Dulong-Petit law, with a 5% elemental deficiency taken into account for the deficient films. The uncertainty in the measured total thermal conductivity is estimated to be within 8%.

Flexible TE device fabrication and measurement
To fabricate a nine-leg flexible thin-film thermoelectric generator, nine rectangular α-MgAgSb thermoelectric legs (6 mm in length, 2 mm in width, and 400 nm in thickness) were deposited on a PI substrate using a stainless-steel shadow mask. Thereafter, Ag interconnects with a thickness of 100 nm were deposited in MBE at room temperature to electrically connect the nine pairs of thermoelectric legs. The α-MgAgSb legs were fabricated using the same thin-film deposition procedure described above, with the deposition time extended to achieve a thickness of 400 nm. To evaluate the performance of the flexible thin-film thermoelectric generator, the device was mounted at the edge of a heating stage, with one side in contact with the stage and the other side exposed to air. By controlling the stage temperature, different temperature gradients across the two ends of the thermoelectric legs were established. The TE device performance was evaluated using a KEITHLEY 2400 Source Measuring Unit, which measured the I-V characteristics to calculate the power output of the TE device.

First-principles calculations
The electronic band structures of α-MgAgSb with and without elemental deficiencies were calculated using the Vienna ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) software. The generalized gradient approximation of Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (GGA-PBE) combined with the modified Becke-Johnson (mBJ) exchange-correlation functional was employed63,64. After full geometry relaxation, self-consistent static calculations were performed on 64-atom α-MgAgSb unit cell (Mg16Ag16Sb16) and on deficient structures, namely Mg15Ag16Sb16, Mg16Ag15Sb16, Mg16Ag16Sb15 for Mg-, Ag- and Sb-deficient cases at the 16i, 8e, 16i Wyckoff sites, respectively. A plane-wave energy cutoff of 500 eV was used, and the Hellmann-Feynman force on each atom energy was converged below 0.001 eV·Å−1, with an electronic convergence criterion of 10-8 eV. The resulting band structures were unfolded back to the primitive cell using VASPKIT for subsequent analysis65.

TE device evaluation
The temperature difference across the flexible TE device during heating is calculated by using ΔT=Voc/SNleg, following literature methods9,29,32. This approach could reflect the effective temperature difference experienced by the device, where Voc is the open-circuit voltage of the device under temperature difference, S is the Seebeck coefficient of the p-type leg at the hot-side temperature, and Nleg is the number of TE legs in the device. The Seebeck coefficient at the cold side differs from that at the hot side, which will introduce some uncertainty in ΔT. However, for the maximum temperature gradient of ~40K, this difference is within 6%. Considering the instrumental uncertainty in Seebeck coefficient measurements, the overall uncertainty in the estimated ΔT will be within 10%. The output power density is calculated by using P=V·I/A, where A is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the direction of heat flow in the device. The normalized maximum power density is calculated as Pmax/AΔT2 with an estimated uncertainty of approximately 12%.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors report the fabrication of flexible, phase-pure α-MgAgSb thin films that exhibit high thermoelectric performance (zT ≈ 0.8 at 300 K; PF ≈ 19.3 µW cm-1 K-2 at 473 K), achieved through molecular-beam deposition. The study highlights the stabilization of the α-phase, controlled stoichiometry, and good mechanical robustness, representing a substantial improvement over traditional Bi2Te3-based flexible films. However, the manuscript requires significant improvement in its overall organization and in the interpretation of the experimental data. The following comments should be addressed to facilitate further consideration of the manuscript.
1. The introduction is too lengthy and should focus more directly on the main research gap, specifically regarding the phase-pure, high-performance flexible α-MgAgSb films. The background information on organic and hybrid thermoelectrics, as well as the discussion on plasticity and size-reduction strategies, can be significantly condensed. When referring to other example systems, their key limitations should be stated briefly and clearly. The authors should avoid subjective terms such as “excellent”, “best”, or “unprecedented”, and should appropriately qualify their claims of novelty. Additionally, the overall text should be carefully revised for grammar and clarity.
2. The reported zT at 300 K is impressive for a flexible film, but it is still lower than that of Bi2Te3. The power factor is also comparatively low; therefore, the authors should emphasize the zT at 300 K and the higher PF at 473 K while ensuring a fair comparison at the same temperature. The discussion lacks an analysis of the underlying transport mechanisms and how they relate to the observed increases in PF and zT. Although Figures 1d–f are presented clearly, the authors should provide a brief explanation of how the transport mechanisms in α-MgAgSb differ from those in the comparison materials to offer a more comprehensive physical interpretation.
3. The increase in Seebeck coefficient for the Sb-deficient samples is likely due to a reduction in hole concentration, which can be demonstrated using the using the S–nH relation. The authors should also provide a brief explanation for why all deficient films exhibit lower PF, even though some show a reduced κ. In the thermal conductivity analysis, it is important to address the potential influence of interfacial thermal resistance between the MgAgSb film and the Pt transducer, as this can significantly affect TDTR measurements in ultrathin films. Additionally, using a fixed specific heat may introduce systematic errors, especially for nanostructured or off-stoichiometric samples. This assumption should either be justified or its uncertainty should be estimated. The analysis would improve by separating and discussing the contributions of electronic and lattice contributions to κ, which would help clarify the roles of carrier and phonon transport.
4. Isotropy must be demonstrated by directional measurements or validated by calculations, rather than relying solely on grain size. The statement “nanoscale grains suggest isotropic TE performance” is speculative and should be supported by appropriate references. The authors need to clarify the dual role of nanoscale grains, explaining how they reduce κ via enhanced phonon scattering while potentially degrading electrical transport through grain-boundary scattering. While the bending test is useful, it has its limitations. If possible, the strain should be estimated based on the bending radius and the thickness of the film/substrate. Additionally, post-bending SEM images should be provided to confirm the absence of cracks, delamination, or failures in interconnects. The authors should also specify the temperature difference used for device performance normalization and discuss the associated uncertainties to ensure a fair comparison between devices.
5. The conclusion is somewhat repetitive and relies too heavily on phrases such as “for the first time”, “excellent”, and “unprecedented”. The statement that zT may exceed 1 at higher temperatures is speculative, as no data beyond 523 K are provided; the authors should clarify the basis for this expectation. While the discussion of device performance is clear, the term “unprecedented” should be avoided unless it is backed by a direct numerical comparison with the best-performing flexible devices in the literature. Instead of concluding with repeated praise, the conclusion would be stronger if it included a more forward-looking perspective on future studies.
6. In the Film fabrication section, the temperature control needs to be described more precisely. Since the stabilization of the α-MgAgSb phase is highly sensitive to temperature, it is important to specify the actual substrate temperature range rather than just the set temperature. The authors state that deposition time was adjusted to obtain ~180 nm films, but they do not provide information on the deposition rate or thickness uniformity. Small variations in Mg flux can lead to the formation of secondary phases, making these details crucial. Although QCM flux monitoring is mentioned, it remains unclear whether post-deposition compositional analysis, such as EDS or XPS quantification, was performed to confirm the stoichiometry of the films. Given the sensitivity of MgAgSb to the flux ratio, it is essential to state the nominal atomic flux ratio (e.g., Mg:Ag:Sb = 1:1:1) and to explain how this ratio was adjusted for stoichiometric versus element-deficient films.
7. In the Characterization section, the authors should specify whether XRD was performed in grazing-incidence mode, which is more appropriate for ~180 nm films on polymer substrates. Regarding thickness measurement, the step-profile method is acceptable; however, the procedure for creating the step and the associated uncertainty should be clearly stated. The description of the Hall measurement is incomplete; it should include details about the magnetic field strength and the measurement geometry. Additionally, issues such as contact stability and the influence of the substrate should be briefly addressed. For the ZEM-3 measurements, the authors should provide the sample dimensions used in the measurement fixture and include a concise statement on data reproducibility across multiple samples to confirm the reliability of the reported results.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript, the authors present high-performance MgAgSb-based flexible thermoelectric film and device. By employing molecular beam deposition and finely manipulating the composition, they successfully achieved a phase-pure α-MgAgSb film, leading to a high power factor. The as-fabricated device also demonstrates a high normalized output power density. This work makes a great contribution to the development of high-performance flexible thermoelectrics with an unusual way. The manuscript is well organized, and the experimental results convincingly support the discussion and conclusions. I would like to recommend this work after addressing the following comments:
1. Besides molecular beam deposition, are there any other feasible methods to fabricate MgAgSb thin films? Since molecular beam epitaxy is a complex and expensive equipment that may limit scalability.
2. Although a phase-pure film was obtained, the reported power factor is still slightly lower than that of the corresponding bulk material. Please give some explanations.
3. The authors report that a 5% elemental deficiency results in a noticeable degradation of thermoelectric performance. Since this deficiency is relatively large, it would be interesting to know whether smaller deviations in composition might have a different impact on the film properties.
4. In the device measurement, the hot-side temperature reached up to 513 K. This temperature appears higher than what is typically expected for flexible electronic device applications. Would that be harmful to the flexible device?
5. In Fig. 4f, a finger touch generates an open-circuit voltage of about 3 mV. Recent studies have reported practical evaluations of power density for flexible thermoelectric generators under similar human-body heat conditions (e.g. Chem. Mater. 31 2019, 5238-5244.). Could the authors estimate or calculate the corresponding output power density based on the device resistance?
6. There exist some typos, e.g. “A more promising route is to fabricate α-MgAgSb thin films via through bottom-up approaches.” The authors should carefully scrutinize the manuscript to avoid similar mistakes.

Comment 1: Besides molecular beam deposition, are there any other feasible methods
to fabricate MgAgSb thin films? Since molecular beam epitaxy is a complex and
expensive equipment that may limit scalability.
Response: Thank you for this constructive suggestion and insightful question. The
main challenge in fabricating MgAgSb thin films lies in the precise control of
stoichiometry and the complete reaction of all constituent elements. For this reason, we
adopted molecular beam deposition using molecular beam epitaxy equipment, which
enables accurate flux control and stable growth conditions. We agree that, in addition
to molecular beam epitaxy, other thin-film fabrication techniques such as pulsed laser
deposition and sol-gel processing may in principle be applicable to MgAgSb films, as
they could also enable stoichiometry control and facilitate growth of the α phase. We
also acknowledge that molecular beam epitaxy systems are complex and costly, which
may limit scalability. However, by demonstrating the feasibility of growing high-
performance flexible MgAgSb thin films, future optimization using more scalable
deposition techniques can be expected. This forward-looking perspective has been
added to the revised manuscript on Page 14: “In future studies, strategies such as grain
enlargement and doping could be explored to further enhance thermoelectric
performance, as the current films still underperform compared with optimized bulk
materials. Moreover, developing scalable, large-area fabrication routes and integrating
these films into flexible device architectures will be crucial for more practical
applications.”
Comment 2: Although a phase-pure film was obtained, the reported power factor is
still slightly lower than that of the corresponding bulk material. Please give some
explanations.
Response: Thank you very much for this valuable comment. In general, the
thermoelectric performance of thin films is often lower than that of corresponding bulk
materials, mainly due to reduced carrier mobility arising from defects, impurities, and
structural disorder. We appreciate your observation that, although our films are phase-
pure, their power factor remains slightly lower than that of bulk MgAgSb. We attribute
this difference primarily to the small grain size in the films, which enhances grain-
boundary scattering and leads to lower carrier mobility compared with state-of-the-art
bulk MgAgSb reported in the literature. Despite this reduction in carrier mobility, the
nanoscale grain size, typically below 100 nm, effectively suppresses lattice thermal
conductivity, thereby helping to maintain a relatively high zT in the thin films. This
trade-off between electrical and thermal transport has now been explicitly discussed in
the revised manuscript on Page 10: “Notably, although all these films exhibit a reduced
κ compared with bulk samples due to enhanced phonon scattering from nanoscale
L
grains, such nanoscale grains can also induce carrier scattering, leading to a relatively
lower carrier mobility than that of bulk counterparts50 and consequently relatively low
zT values.”

intentionally selected a relatively large elemental deficiency of 5% to clearly illustrate

transport properties, providing a boundary for how compositional deviation affects
material performance. We agree that a 5% deficiency may be relatively large for
practical applications. For smaller deviations in composition, the impact on
thermoelectric properties is expected to be less pronounced and unlikely to exceed the
trends observed here. Nevertheless, even small Sb deficiency should be avoided in
practice, as it can significantly modify the band structure near the valence band

and overall thermoelectric performance. A brief discussion addressing this point has
now been added to the revised manuscript: “Overall, stoichiometric films exhibit the
best TE performance among α-MgAgSb thin films, and even slight Sb deficiency should
be avoided whenever possible.”

polyimide substrate provides mechanical support and redistributes bending induced
stress, effectively reducing the strain experienced by the film during deformation. The

## Abstract

Flexible thermoelectric materials hold great promise for sustainable energy supply in flexible electronics. However, beyond the long-standing champion Bi2Te3-based flexible films, high-performance alternatives remain scarce. Here, we report a promising flexible thermoelectric material based on eco-friendly MgAgSb, a bulk-proven high-performance system whose development in flexible form has long been hindered by its intrinsic brittleness and phase complexity. Using molecular beam deposition, we manage to precisely stabilize MgAgSb within its α-phase range and finely control its stoichiometry. As a result, we successfully fabricate the α-MgAgSb film with exceptional performance, achieving a room temperature zT of 0.8 and a peak power factor of 19.3 μW cm-1 K-2, ranking among the promising flexible thermoelectric materials developed. Moreover, the α-MgAgSb film is revealed to exhibit notable flexibility and stability under repeated bending and heating. Leveraging this high-performance stable α-MgAgSb film, the flexible thermoelectric device delivers a maximum normalized power density of 4.9 μW cm-2 K-2. This work opens a pathway for flexible MgAgSb applications and offers strong potential for realizing self-powered flexible technologies.

---

## Introduction

Flexible electronics are emerging technologies that enable advancements in wearable devices, healthcare monitoring, and soft robotics, while also opening new possibilities for applications in high-temperature environments above 373K, such as aerospace surface monitoring and engine diagnostics1. However, continuously and maintenance-free powering of electronic components within flexible devices remains a critical challenge2. Thermoelectric (TE) devices, which can directly harvest heat from surfaces and the environment to generate sustainable electrical energy, offer a promising alternative to traditional batteries3–5. Typically, TE devices consist of n-type and p-type TE materials connected in series to convert heat into electricity, and their conversion efficiency is fundamentally determined by the dimensionless figure of merit (zT) of the constituent TE materials6. zT is defined as zT = S2σT/κ = PF × T/κ, where S is the Seebeck coefficient, σ is the electrical conductivity, κ is the total thermal conductivity, PF (= S2σ) is the power factor, a metric of electrical performance. It means that achieving high zT requires materials with both a high PF and a low κ. Beyond high TE performance, in the context of flexible thermoelectrics, the mechanical flexibility of TE materials and devices is also a key prerequisite7,8.

However, flexibility and TE performance are two different material attributes. Achieving both high flexibility and high TE performance in a single material remains highly challenging, making suitable candidates for flexible thermoelectrics extremely scarce9. Organic thermoelectric (TE) materials offer excellent flexibility due to their molecular and polymeric structures, but suffer from low electrical performance10. Although significant efforts have been devoted to enhancing systems such as PEDOT: PSS11–13, PANI14, SWCNT15,16, and PMHJ17, their zT and PF values remain far below those of inorganic TE materials. Hybridizing organics with inorganics can provide moderate performance and flexibility, but weak interfacial bonding and still-inferior TE properties hinder practical use18,19. To date, inorganic TE compounds remain the leaders in TE performance, with materials such as SnSe and GeTe achieving zT values exceeding 220–24. However, their brittleness limits flexible applications.

Reducing the dimensional size of materials to the micro- or nanoscale is an effective approach to endow brittle materials with flexibility through either top-down or bottom-up methods9,25–27. Top-down processing is often limited by their intrinsic brittleness. Only a few inorganic compounds, including Ag2(S, Se, Te)9,26,28, Mg3(Sb, Bi)229, single-crystalline Bi2Te330 and some van der Waals compounds31 exhibit intrinsic plasticity that enables safer deformation and flexible device fabrication32–34. In most cases, bottom-up synthesis of thin films (e.g., by printing or various deposition) is preferred, offering flexibility and tunability35,36. Currently, research on thin-film-based flexible inorganic TE materials has mainly focused on Bi2Te337–39 and Ag2Se40–42 due to their superior room temperature TE performance. For instance, p-type Bi0.3Sb1.7Te3 can achieve a zT value exceeding 1 at room temperature43, while n-type Ag2Se exhibits a comparable performance under similar conditions40. However, their performance deteriorates rapidly at elevated temperatures, posing an obstacle for their applications in flexible devices operating above 373K. Furthermore, the toxicity of Te/Se and the scarcity of Te impose additional limitations on their practical deployment44.

In contrast, α-MgAgSb is an eco-friendly and high-performance TE material, exhibiting zT values of ~0.8 at room temperature and peak values of around 1.3 above 473K45. Its intrinsically high PF across the working temperature range stems from its high band degeneracy, while its complex crystal structure results in its intrinsically low lattice thermal conductivity46,47. These merits make α-MgAgSb one of the most promising p-type TE materials near room temperature, particularly as a potential substitute for p-type (Bi, Sb)2Te3 in power generation. However, the TE performance of α-MgAgSb is highly sensitive to impurities such as Ag3Sb48, and α-MgAgSb will also undergo phase transitions to β- and γ-MgAgSb at elevated temperatures, complicating the fabrication of high-performance α-MgAgSb. Many processing optimizations have been reported to improve the phase purity and reliability of bulk α-MgAgSb, advancing its use in rigid TE devices45,49.

Despite these encouraging developments, studies on α-MgAgSb have so far been limited to rigid bulk forms, leaving its application in flexible thermoelectrics largely unexplored.

α-MgAgSb is intrinsically brittle, making it particularly difficult to impart flexibility through top-down processing methods. A more promising route is to fabricate α-MgAgSb thin films via bottom-up approaches. However, the complex phase behavior of MgAgSb poses significant challenges for film fabrication, and achieving flexible α-MgAgSb films with high performance remains elusive. In previous work, Wang et al.50 prepared flexible MgAgSb-based films by solution-casting mixtures of α-MgAgSb powder with graphene and PEDOT:PSS. However, the presence of multiple phases and interfaces in such inorganic/organic composites led to TE performance far below that of bulk α-MgAgSb. Besides, Oueldna et al. attempted to co-deposit Mg, Ag and Sb using magnetron sputtering. However, regardless of how the initial composition ratio was adjusted, the resulting films failed to form pure α-MgAgSb as the main phase51,52. At present, despite the promising TE potential of α-MgAgSb, a phase-pure and high-performance α-MgAgSb film suitable for flexible TE devices has not yet been realized.

In this work, we employ molecular beam deposition to precisely stabilize MgAgSb within its α-phase range and finely tune its stoichiometry. This deposition technique provides a quasi-equilibrium growth environment that favors the formation of phase-pure α-MgAgSb while suppressing secondary phases. Consequently, we successfully obtain the flexible inorganic α-MgAgSb thin film with exceptional TE performance, achieving a zT value of 0.8 at room temperature and a peak PF of 19.3 μW cm−1 K-2 at 473K, placing these films among the promising flexible p-type TE candidates beyond Bi2Te3. Using this technique, we further investigate the impact of stoichiometric deviations and find that slight deficiencies in composition degrade the TE performance of α-MgAgSb. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the fabricated α-MgAgSb film exhibits notable flexibility and thermal stability, maintains performance after 1000 bending cycles and repeated thermal cycling between 373K and 473K. Finally, we fabricate a flexible thermoelectric device based on these films, realizing an estimated normalized power density of 4.9 μW cm-2 K-2, suggesting their strong practical potential. This work marks an important step in the exploration of flexible α-MgAgSb and provides valuable insights for integrating MgAgSb-based thermoelectrics in flexible electronics.

---

## Results

High-performance flexible α-MgAgSb film
MgAgSb exhibits three polymorphs over different temperature ranges: α-MgAgSb, β-MgAgSb, and γ-MgAgSb. Among them, only α-MgAgSb shows high TE potential with large zT values, whereas both β- and γ-MgAgSb display poor performance. A recent study has demonstrated that β-MgAgSb can be strategically utilized in α/β-segmented junctions to enhance power output while maintaining conversion efficiency53. However, the formation of β- or especially γ-MgAgSb within the MgAgSb matrix will degrade its overall TE performance. As shown in Fig. 1a, γ-MgAgSb forms from β-MgAgSb upon heating, accompanied by the precipitation of Ag3Sb and Sb. Once γ-MgAgSb, Ag3Sb, and Sb appear, they remain even after cooling to room temperature, which not only deteriorates MgAgSb performance but also complicates the synthesis of high-quality MgAgSb. This issue is particularly critical for film fabrication. Magnetron sputtering, a commonly used deposition technique, has consistently failed to produce high-performance α-MgAgSb films because of extensive impurity formation. Typically, during sputtering, energetic atoms, ions, and excited species with high kinetic energies and fluctuating fluxes lead to non-uniform nucleation and far-from-equilibrium growth, making the formation of secondary phases easy. These problems are particularly severe for MgAgSb due to the above-mentioned complex phase behavior. In addition, the high vapor pressure and reactivity of Mg under the relatively low vacuum of the sputtering chamber result in Mg loss and undesired reactions during deposition, which further disturb the stoichiometry and hinder precise phase control, making it difficult to fabricate high-performance MgAgSb films.

To achieve a high-performance α-MgAgSb film, precise phase control during deposition is essential. First, the reaction temperature must be strictly maintained below 573K to keep MgAgSb within the α-phase stability range. Second, the deposited Mg, Ag and Sb atoms need to thoroughly react under near-equilibrium conditions. Third, a high-vacuum environment is required to prevent oxidation and undesirable reactions of Mg. Based on these requirements, we employed molecular beam deposition (Fig. 1b), which offers ideal growth conditions for the MgAgSb film. In this process, low-energy neutral Mg, Ag and Sb atoms arrive at the substrate in well-collimated molecular beams under ultra-high vacuum. The slow and gentle deposition enables controlled surface diffusion and reaction of these atoms under quasi-equilibrium conditions, forming α-MgAgSb when the substrate temperature is maintained at 523K. It is worth noting that although a molecular beam epitaxy system was used, the substrate was a flexible polyimide rather than a conventional single-crystalline substrate, which enables both film growth and mechanical flexibility. Supplementary Fig. S1 shows the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the molecular-beam-deposited films, which match well with the corresponding powder diffraction patterns of the α-MgAgSb phase, confirming that flexible α-MgAgSb films were successfully obtained on polyimide substrates (Fig. 1c).

Importantly, as shown in Fig. 1d, the flexible MgAgSb films exhibit an excellent room-temperature zT of 0.8. Although this value is slightly lower than that of state-of-the-art p-type Bi2Te3-based flexible materials, it is significantly higher than those of other reported flexible TE films. Moreover, as shown in Fig. 1e, the α-MgAgSb film shows an increasing PF, reaching a maximum of 19.3 μW cm−1 K−2 at 473K. This temperature-dependent enhancement leads to a high average power factor (PFavg) of 17.2 μW cm−1 K−2 over the range of 293–523K (Fig. 1f). The exceptional performance (zT and PF) of α-MgAgSb in this work can be attributed to the successful synthesis of high-purity α-MgAgSb. Intrinsically, the favorable band structure of high band degeneracy, as well as large anharmonicity and weak chemical bonding in α-MgAgSb, enables its high PF and zT compared to other materials. These results highlight the strong potential of flexible α-MgAgSb films for TE applications even beyond room temperature.

Elemental deficiency effects on TE performance
MgAgSb is known to be highly sensitive to stoichiometry54. Molecular beam deposition provides an ideal platform to investigate how stoichiometric deviation affects the TE performance of flexible MgAgSb film. By carefully adjusting the flux rate of Mg, Ag and Sb (Supplementary Fig. S2 and Supplementary Table S1), we intentionally introduced a 5% deficiency in each element to allow a clearer observation of the effects of non-stoichiometry on the TE properties of MgAgSb thin films, producing Mg-deficient, Ag-deficient, and Sb-deficient films, respectively. XRD patterns confirmed that all these films remain primarily in the α-MgAgSb phase (Supplementary Fig. S3). The TE performance of these films was systematically measured over a temperature range of 303K to 523K to assess the impact of these deficiencies, with the corresponding thickness data shown in Supplementary Fig. S4. As shown in Fig. 2a, Sb and Ag deficiencies lead to higher resistivity ρ of the films, whereas Mg deficiency decreases ρ. Figure 2b shows the S of these films, and the S increases in the Sb-deficient, slightly decreases in Ag-deficient films, and drops markedly in the Mg-deficient film. Consequently, all deficient films exhibit lower PF than the stoichiometric film (Fig. 2c), underscoring the critical role of precise phase and composition control in achieving high-performance α-MgAgSb films.

To further elucidate the impact of elemental deficiencies on charge transport, we measured the Hall carrier concentration nH and mobility μH of each α-MgAgSb film at room temperature. As shown in Fig. 2d, the stoichiometric film exhibits an nH of 3.9 × 1019 cm−3 and a μH of 53 cm2 V−1 s−1, values consistent with those reported for high-performance bulk α-MgAgSb55. For the element-deficient films, Sb deficiency is observed to reduce the room-temperature nH, which may arise from the formation of Sb vacancies (V3+Sb). These vacancies act as electron donors, leading to a decreased nH and consequently an increased S according to the Pisarenko relation. In the case of Ag deficiency, Ag vacancies (V−Ag) may be induced, increasing nH, as reflected by the decreasing trend of S over a broad temperature range. In contrast, Mg deficiency markedly increases nH due to the formation of Mg vacancies (V2−Mg) and Ag-Mg antistites defects (AgMg)56,57, resulting in a much lower S. Notably, μH decreases uniformly in all deficient films, primarily due to enhanced carrier scattering from point defects and possible secondary phases associated with non-stoichiometry. The reduced μH intrinsically deteriorates electrical transport, resulting in all deficient films exhibiting lower PFs than the non-deficient sample. Since charge transport is also strongly influenced by the electronic band structure, we further investigated how elemental deficiencies modify the band structure of α-MgAgSb. As shown in Fig. 2e, Ag and Mg deficiencies exert little influence on the valence band maximum (VBM) between the X and Γ points, whereas Sb deficiency significantly distorts the VBM. This distortion likely explains the pronounced reduction in mobility observed in Sb-deficient films. Overall, among the various elemental deficiencies, Sb deficiency is the most detrimental, leading to both the lowest carrier nH and μH, and thus causing the greatest degradation in electrical performance, with the PF of the Sb-deficient film being only half that of the non-deficient film.

In addition to electrical performance, the cross-plane thermal conductivity κ of these films was measured at room temperature using the time-domain thermoreflectance method and is presented in Supplementary Figs. S5, S6 and Supplementary Table S2. All films exhibit lower κ compared to reported bulk values. The non-deficient MgAgSb film shows a κ of 0.61 W m−1 K−1, while the deficient films show even lower values. Benefiting from the ultralow κ and relatively high PF, the non-deficient flexible MgAgSb film achieves a room-temperature zT of approximately 0.8, which is comparable to that of state-of-the-art MgAgSb bulk. However, despite the lower κ values in element-deficient films, all of them exhibit reduced zT values. In particular, the zT of the Sb-deficient film drops to around 0.5 at room temperature (Supplementary Fig. S7), primarily due to its pronounced decline in PF.

Microstructure, stability and flexibility of α-MgAgSb film
MgAgSb is intrinsically a low κ system. The α-MgAgSb films fabricated by molecular beam deposition exhibit lower κ than most conventional bulk α-MgAgSb, as noted in the previous section55. To elucidate the origin of their low κ, we examined the microstructures of stoichiometric and element-deficient films using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). As shown in Fig. 3a and Supplementary Figs. S8, S9, the stoichiometric, Ag‑deficient, and Mg‑deficient films display uniform and compact surfaces, whereas the Sb‑deficient film shows poor and uneven crystal quality, indicating that Sb deficiency is unfavorable for the growth of α-MgAgSb crystals. Notably, the grains in all films are nanosized; for example, the stoichiometric film has grain sizes of about 60-90 nm, as displayed in Fig. 3b. The nanoscale grain structure reveals the polycrystalline nature of the films. Together with the absence of obvious preferred orientation in the XRD patterns (Supplementary Fig S1), the films are therefore expected to exhibit nearly isotropic TE properties, even though S and σ were measured in-plane, while κ was measured cross-plane. These nanoscale grains result from the low deposition temperature, which limits atomic diffusion and grain growth. To further investigate compositional uniformity, we also applied the energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis. As shown in Fig. 3c and Supplementary Figs. S10–S12, Mg, Ag and Sb are homogeneously distributed in the stoichiometric, Ag-deficient, and Mg-deficient films. In contrast, the Sb-deficient film contains Mg-rich regions (Supplementary Fig. S12), evidencing impurity formation.

To gain deeper insight into the impact of elemental deficiencies on thermal transport, we have decomposed the total thermal conductivity into its electronic and lattice components (Supplementary Note S1 and Supplementary Fig. S13). It is evident that Sb deficiency leads to an increase in lattice thermal conductivity (κL), whereas Mg deficiency results in a pronounced reduction in κL. In comparison, Ag deficiency has a relatively minor influence on κL. The increased κL observed in Sb-deficient films likely originates from the formation of Mg-rich metallic secondary phases, as evidenced in Supplementary Figs. S9 and S12. In contrast, the presence of Mg vacancies and Ag-Mg antisite defects in Mg-deficient films enhances phonon scattering, thereby reducing κL48. Notably, although all these films exhibit a reduced κL compared with bulk samples due to enhanced phonon scattering from nanoscale grains, such nanoscale grains can also induce carrier scattering, leading to a relatively lower carrier mobility than that of bulk counterparts49 and consequently relatively low zT values.

Overall, stoichiometric films exhibit the best TE performance among α-MgAgSb thin films, and even slight Sb deficiency should be avoided whenever possible. In addition to high performance of the stoichiometric films, thermal stability and mechanical stability are essential for their practical applications in flexible electronics38. We first evaluated the thermal stability of the film under repeated measurements at 373K and 473K (the temperature of peak PF). As shown in Fig. 3d, the electrical transport properties, including the S, σ, and PF, remain unchanged, demonstrating excellent thermal stability under elevated-temperature operation. This stability can be attributed to the intrinsic phase stability of α-MgAgSb, which is thermodynamically stable over a broad temperature range and does not undergo phase transitions or decomposition within the temperature window investigated in this work58. We then assessed the flexibility of the α-MgAgSb film by subjecting it to repeated bending at a fixed bending radius of 10 mm, corresponding to an applied strain of approximately 0.75% (Supplementary Note S2 and Fig. 3e). The ratios of S/S0, σ/σ0, and PF/PF0 (where S0, σ0, and PF0 are the initial values) are found to remain nearly constant with increasing bending cycles. Remarkably, after 1000 bending cycles, the PF of the film retains 96% of its initial value within a 5% measurement error. The surface morphology after 1000 bending cycles (Supplementary Fig. S14) shows few cracks. These results confirm the excellent flexibility and durability of the α-MgAgSb film. This high flexibility arises from the small film thickness (about 180 nm), which allows large elastic bending strains25, together with the intrinsically flexible polyimide substrate that redistributes bending-induced stress and reduces the effective strain in the film. Consequently, the α-MgAgSb films show strong potential for flexible TE power generation under practical operating conditions, including applications requiring mechanical compliance and thermal robustness.

High-performance flexible α-MgAgSb TE device
To evaluate the practical potential of the flexible α-MgAgSb film, we fabricated a flexible TE device consisting of nine MgAgSb legs electrically connected in series using Ag interconnects (Fig. 4a). For power generation, one side of the flexible TE device is heated, enabling in-plane heat flow. Based on this configuration, we measured the open-circuit voltage (Voc) generated by the TE device and the output power under different hot-side temperatures with varying loading current (I). As shown in Fig. 4b, when the hot-side temperature is 393K (estimated ΔT=16K), the Voc reaches 40 mV. As the hot-side temperature increases to 513K (estimated ΔT=40K), the Voc rises to 66 mV. The relationship between Voc and ΔT is shown in Supplementary Fig. S15, clearly demonstrating that Voc of TE device increases with ΔT. Based on the measured output voltage and current, the output power was calculated. The maximum output power (Pmax) is achieved when the internal resistance of the device matches the external load resistance, as shown in Supplementary Fig. S16. Consequently, a normalized power density (Pmax/AΔT2) of 4.9 μW cm−2 K−2 is obtained at a hot-side temperature of 513K. As shown in Fig. 4c and Supplementary Table S3, the normalized power density achieved in this work ranks among the leading values ever reported for flexible in-plane TE devices based on other material systems, highlighting the excellent potential of α-MgAgSb for flexible energy conversion applications. Notably, the device operates reliably at elevated temperatures up to 513K, making it suitable not only for wearable electronics but also for practical applications such as aerospace surface monitoring, engine diagnostics, and smart factories, where moderate temperature gradients are available.

To further reveal the flexibility of the device, we measured the output voltage and output power under bending conditions, as shown in Supplementary Fig. S17. At a hot stage temperature of 513K, the Voc is 58 mV, and the Pmax reaches 0.36 μW. It should be noted that the flexible TE device was mounted on the curved surface of a carbon pillar rather than directly on a flat heating stage, resulting in a different effective hot-side temperature on the device and, consequently, variations in the measured output voltage and power. In addition to testing under curved-surface conditions, we further evaluated the mechanical flexibility of the flexible MgAgSb TE device through repeated bending tests. Unlike a single TE film, a TE device includes additional electrical contacts, making such tests essential. As shown in Fig. 4d, after 1000 bending cycles with a fixed bending radius of 10 mm, the device’s internal resistance R increased only slightly by about 6% compared to its initial internal resistance R0. Meanwhile, the Pmax/A after 1000 bending cycles remained almost unchanged compared to its initial value (Fig. 4e). These results demonstrate the excellent flexibility and reliability of the device for potential practical flexible TE applications. To further illustrate its potential, we tested the device under finger-induced temperature gradients. As shown in Fig. 4f, g, the device generated an output voltage of about 3.0 mV and a maximum output power of 0.88 nW when placed on the side or tip of a finger, highlighting its promise for wearable technology and paving the way for flexible TE devices as sustainable power sources for flexible electronics59.

In summary, by succeeding to precisely stabilizing MgAgSb within its α-phase range and finely controlling its composition using advanced molecular beam deposition, we have successfully fabricated high-performance flexible α-MgAgSb films. This flexible α-MgAgSb film achieves a zT value of 0.8 at room temperature and a PF of 19.3 μW cm−1 K−2 at 473K, surpassing most flexible TE materials and second only to the long-standing champion, flexible Bi2Te3 films. Notably, the PF of flexible α-MgAgSb film increases with temperature, leading to an excellent average PF of 17.2 μW cm−1 K−2 in the 293–523K range. This measured increase in PF with temperature, together with the expected decrease in thermal conductivity at elevated temperatures due to enhanced phonon scattering, suggests that zT values exceeding 0.8 may be achievable at higher temperatures. Beyond its high performance, the flexible α-MgAgSb film shows remarkable thermal stability and mechanical flexibility under thermal and bending cycles. Finally, a flexible TE device comprising nine α-MgAgSb film legs is demonstrated to exhibit an estimated normalized power density of 4.9 μW cm−2 K−2, demonstrating strong potential for power generation in flexible electronics. In future studies, strategies such as grain enlargement and doping could be explored to further enhance TE performance, as the current films still underperform compared with optimized bulk materials. Moreover, developing scalable, large-area fabrication routes and integrating these films into flexible device architectures will be crucial for more practical applications. Nevertheless, this work opens a new pathway for flexible applications of α-MgAgSb and represents an important step toward self-powered flexible technologies.
