## Methods

Film fabrication
All flexible α-MgAgSb films were deposited on a polyimide substrate using a molecular beam epitaxy system (EV-500, Eiko). The base pressure in the chamber was 10⁻⁸ Pa, and the working pressure was maintained in the 10-7 Pa range during deposition. Mg, Ag, and Sb of 4N purity were placed in separate Knudsen cells and heated to the specified temperatures. The evaporation rate of each element was determined using a retractable quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) thickness monitor (Q-pod, Inficon), located at the substrate position. The substrate was heated from the back of the sample stage. A thermocouple measured the temperature between the sample holder and the heater, which controlled the heater power to keep a specified temperature. The actual substrate temperature was consistent with the set temperature when the temperature was below 773K. The polyimide substrate was immersed in acetone and subjected to ultrasonic cleaning for 30 minutes to remove surface organic contaminants and dust before being transferred into the vacuum chamber. It was heated to 523K and held for 30 minutes to remove residual impurities before deposition. The α-MgAgSb films were prepared by co-depositing Mg, Ag, and Sb with a 1:1:1 flux ratio, monitored by a QCM, at a substrate temperature of 523K. Compositional analysis was performed by EDS on films deposited on Al2O3 substrate under the same conditions as those on polyimide. As shown in Supplementary Fig. S18 and Supplementary Table S4, the film composition closely matches the intended 1:1:1 ratio. Based on this result, off-stoichiometric films were fabricated by individually reducing the flux of each element by 5% during deposition. EDS analysis further confirms a ~5% Sb deficiency in the corresponding film (Supplementary Fig. S18 and Supplementary Table S4). The films were deposited at a rate of 6 nm per minute for 30 min with the substrate rotating at 5 rpm, resulting in a thickness of approximately 180 nm.

Characterization
The phase composition and crystallinity of the stoichiometric MgAgSb film were examined using XRD and grazing incidence XRD (GIXRD). XRD measurements were performed on a Rigaku MiniFlex diffractometer with a Cu Kα+β source, while GIXRD was carried out using a Rigaku TF-XRD system equipped with a Cu Kα source. Both techniques reveal the characteristic diffraction peaks of the α-MgAgSb phase. Because GIXRD measurements are more time-consuming, conventional XRD, which provides reliable and efficient phase identification, was used for all element-deficient films. The surface morphology of films was analyzed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Hitachi High-Tech/S-4800), and the component was analyzed using energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) (Hitachi High-Tech/TM-3000). The film thicknesses were measured using a surface profiler system (Bruker Dektak 6M) by the step method. The step was created from an uncovered area of the substrate to the film surface. The measurement uncertainty was within 10 nm. Hall carrier concentration and mobility at 300K were measured using a four-probe Hall system (Biorad H5580) under a magnetic field of 0.45 T using the van der Pauw method, which is suitable for samples of arbitrary geometry. The probes were placed at the corners of the film, and the insulating substrate did not affect the measurements. Multiple measurements were performed to ensure stable contacts, with an uncertainty of approximately 1%. The electric conductivity and Seebeck coefficient of thin films were measured using a ZEM-3 (Advance Riko) apparatus in a He atmosphere, with samples having lateral dimensions of 10 mm × 3 mm. Multiple measurements confirmed good reproducibility of the film fabrication, with variations within approximately 5% (Supplementary Fig. S19). The cross-plane thermal conductivity of the samples was measured using the picosecond time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) instrument (PicoTR, PicoTherm) in a front-heating/front-detection configuration. Prior to the measurements, a ~100 nm-thick Pt layer was sputtered onto the thin-film surfaces by using a DC sputtering system to serve as a transducer. A 1550 nm infrared pulsed laser with a repetition frequency of 20 MHz and a pulse duration of 0.5 ps was used as a heat source. A 780 nm probe laser was used to detect the thermoreflectance signal. The picosecond TDTR system was customized to reduce the spot size of the probe laser to ca. 5 μm as described elsewhere60. The improved mirror image method for fitting all the range of pulse interval was used to determine the thermal conductivity value61,62. In Supplementary Fig. S5, the measured thermoreflectance signals are shown together with the fitted curves. The interfacial thermal resistance (ITR) between the MgAgSb film and the Pt layer is extracted to be smaller than 1.0 × 10-8 m2 KW-1 for all films (Supplementary Table S2), indicating that the possible error introduced in film thermal conductivity is at most about 3%. The specific heat of all films was calculated based on the Dulong-Petit law, with a 5% elemental deficiency taken into account for the deficient films. The uncertainty in the measured total thermal conductivity is estimated to be within 8%.

Flexible TE device fabrication and measurement
To fabricate a nine-leg flexible thin-film thermoelectric generator, nine rectangular α-MgAgSb thermoelectric legs (6 mm in length, 2 mm in width, and 400 nm in thickness) were deposited on a PI substrate using a stainless-steel shadow mask. Thereafter, Ag interconnects with a thickness of 100 nm were deposited in MBE at room temperature to electrically connect the nine pairs of thermoelectric legs. The α-MgAgSb legs were fabricated using the same thin-film deposition procedure described above, with the deposition time extended to achieve a thickness of 400 nm. To evaluate the performance of the flexible thin-film thermoelectric generator, the device was mounted at the edge of a heating stage, with one side in contact with the stage and the other side exposed to air. By controlling the stage temperature, different temperature gradients across the two ends of the thermoelectric legs were established. The TE device performance was evaluated using a KEITHLEY 2400 Source Measuring Unit, which measured the I-V characteristics to calculate the power output of the TE device.

First-principles calculations
The electronic band structures of α-MgAgSb with and without elemental deficiencies were calculated using the Vienna ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) software. The generalized gradient approximation of Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (GGA-PBE) combined with the modified Becke-Johnson (mBJ) exchange-correlation functional was employed63,64. After full geometry relaxation, self-consistent static calculations were performed on 64-atom α-MgAgSb unit cell (Mg16Ag16Sb16) and on deficient structures, namely Mg15Ag16Sb16, Mg16Ag15Sb16, Mg16Ag16Sb15 for Mg-, Ag- and Sb-deficient cases at the 16i, 8e, 16i Wyckoff sites, respectively. A plane-wave energy cutoff of 500 eV was used, and the Hellmann-Feynman force on each atom energy was converged below 0.001 eV·Å−1, with an electronic convergence criterion of 10-8 eV. The resulting band structures were unfolded back to the primitive cell using VASPKIT for subsequent analysis65.

TE device evaluation
The temperature difference across the flexible TE device during heating is calculated by using ΔT=Voc/SNleg, following literature methods9,29,32. This approach could reflect the effective temperature difference experienced by the device, where Voc is the open-circuit voltage of the device under temperature difference, S is the Seebeck coefficient of the p-type leg at the hot-side temperature, and Nleg is the number of TE legs in the device. The Seebeck coefficient at the cold side differs from that at the hot side, which will introduce some uncertainty in ΔT. However, for the maximum temperature gradient of ~40K, this difference is within 6%. Considering the instrumental uncertainty in Seebeck coefficient measurements, the overall uncertainty in the estimated ΔT will be within 10%. The output power density is calculated by using P=V·I/A, where A is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the direction of heat flow in the device. The normalized maximum power density is calculated as Pmax/AΔT2 with an estimated uncertainty of approximately 12%.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The authors report the fabrication of flexible, phase-pure α-MgAgSb thin films that exhibit high thermoelectric performance (zT ≈ 0.8 at 300 K; PF ≈ 19.3 µW cm-1 K-2 at 473 K), achieved through molecular-beam deposition. The study highlights the stabilization of the α-phase, controlled stoichiometry, and good mechanical robustness, representing a substantial improvement over traditional Bi2Te3-based flexible films. However, the manuscript requires significant improvement in its overall organization and in the interpretation of the experimental data. The following comments should be addressed to facilitate further consideration of the manuscript.
1. The introduction is too lengthy and should focus more directly on the main research gap, specifically regarding the phase-pure, high-performance flexible α-MgAgSb films. The background information on organic and hybrid thermoelectrics, as well as the discussion on plasticity and size-reduction strategies, can be significantly condensed. When referring to other example systems, their key limitations should be stated briefly and clearly. The authors should avoid subjective terms such as “excellent”, “best”, or “unprecedented”, and should appropriately qualify their claims of novelty. Additionally, the overall text should be carefully revised for grammar and clarity.
2. The reported zT at 300 K is impressive for a flexible film, but it is still lower than that of Bi2Te3. The power factor is also comparatively low; therefore, the authors should emphasize the zT at 300 K and the higher PF at 473 K while ensuring a fair comparison at the same temperature. The discussion lacks an analysis of the underlying transport mechanisms and how they relate to the observed increases in PF and zT. Although Figures 1d–f are presented clearly, the authors should provide a brief explanation of how the transport mechanisms in α-MgAgSb differ from those in the comparison materials to offer a more comprehensive physical interpretation.
3. The increase in Seebeck coefficient for the Sb-deficient samples is likely due to a reduction in hole concentration, which can be demonstrated using the using the S–nH relation. The authors should also provide a brief explanation for why all deficient films exhibit lower PF, even though some show a reduced κ. In the thermal conductivity analysis, it is important to address the potential influence of interfacial thermal resistance between the MgAgSb film and the Pt transducer, as this can significantly affect TDTR measurements in ultrathin films. Additionally, using a fixed specific heat may introduce systematic errors, especially for nanostructured or off-stoichiometric samples. This assumption should either be justified or its uncertainty should be estimated. The analysis would improve by separating and discussing the contributions of electronic and lattice contributions to κ, which would help clarify the roles of carrier and phonon transport.

The statement “nanoscale grains suggest isotropic TE performance” is speculative and should be supported by appropriate references. The authors need to clarify the dual role of nanoscale grains, explaining how they reduce κ via enhanced phonon scattering while potentially degrading electrical transport through grain-boundary scattering. While the bending test is useful, it has its limitations. If possible, the strain should be estimated based on the bending radius and the thickness of the film/substrate. Additionally, post-bending SEM images should be provided to confirm the absence of cracks, delamination, or failures in interconnects. Instead of concluding with repeated praise, the conclusion would be stronger if it included a more forward-looking perspective on future studies.

Comment: In this manuscript, the authors present high-performance MgAgSb-based
flexible thermoelectric film and device. By employing molecular beam deposition and
finely manipulating the composition, they successfully achieved a phase-pure α-

of our work. We sincerely appreciate your constructive comments and helpful
suggestions. In response, we have addressed each point in detail and revised the
manuscript accordingly, as outlined below.
Comment 1: Besides molecular beam deposition, are there any other feasible methods
to fabricate MgAgSb thin films? Since molecular beam epitaxy is a complex and
expensive equipment that may limit scalability.
Response: Thank you for this constructive suggestion and insightful question. The
main challenge in fabricating MgAgSb thin films lies in the precise control of
stoichiometry and the complete reaction of all constituent elements. For this reason, we
adopted molecular beam deposition using molecular beam epitaxy equipment, which
enables accurate flux control and stable growth conditions. We agree that, in addition
to molecular beam epitaxy, other thin-film fabrication techniques such as pulsed laser
deposition and sol-gel processing may in principle be applicable to MgAgSb films, as
they could also enable stoichiometry control and facilitate growth of the α phase. We
also acknowledge that molecular beam epitaxy systems are complex and costly, which
may limit scalability. However, by demonstrating the feasibility of growing high-
performance flexible MgAgSb thin films, future optimization using more scalable
deposition techniques can be expected. This forward-looking perspective has been
added to the revised manuscript on Page 14: “In future studies, strategies such as grain
enlargement and doping could be explored to further enhance thermoelectric
performance, as the current films still underperform compared with optimized bulk
materials. Moreover, developing scalable, large-area fabrication routes and integrating
these films into flexible device architectures will be crucial for more practical
applications.”
Comment 2: Although a phase-pure film was obtained, the reported power factor is
still slightly lower than that of the corresponding bulk material. Please give some
explanations.
Response: Thank you very much for this valuable comment. In general, the
thermoelectric performance of thin films is often lower than that of corresponding bulk
materials, mainly due to reduced carrier mobility arising from defects, impurities, and
structural disorder. We appreciate your observation that, although our films are phase-
pure, their power factor remains slightly lower than that of bulk MgAgSb. We attribute
this difference primarily to the small grain size in the films, which enhances grain-
boundary scattering and leads to lower carrier mobility compared with state-of-the-art
bulk MgAgSb reported in the literature. Despite this reduction in carrier mobility, the
nanoscale grain size, typically below 100 nm, effectively suppresses lattice thermal
conductivity, thereby helping to maintain a relatively high zT in the thin films. This
trade-off between electrical and thermal transport has now been explicitly discussed in
the revised manuscript on Page 10: “Notably, although all these films exhibit a reduced
κ compared with bulk samples due to enhanced phonon scattering from nanoscale
L
grains, such nanoscale grains can also induce carrier scattering, leading to a relatively
lower carrier mobility than that of bulk counterparts50 and consequently relatively low
zT values.”

degradation of thermoelectric performance. Since this deficiency is relatively large, it
would be interesting to know whether smaller deviations in composition might have a
different impact on the film properties.

intentionally selected a relatively large elemental deficiency of 5% to clearly illustrate
the influence of non-stoichiometry on the thermoelectric properties of MgAgSb thin
films. As observed, this level of deficiency leads to a noticeable reduction in electrical
transport properties, providing a boundary for how compositional deviation affects
material performance. We agree that a 5% deficiency may be relatively large for
practical applications. For smaller deviations in composition, the impact on
thermoelectric properties is expected to be less pronounced and unlikely to exceed the
trends observed here. Nevertheless, even small Sb deficiency should be avoided in
practice, as it can significantly modify the band structure near the valence band
maximum and introduce impurity related scattering, which degrades carrier mobility
and overall thermoelectric performance. A brief discussion addressing this point has
now been added to the revised manuscript: “Overall, stoichiometric films exhibit the
best TE performance among α-MgAgSb thin films, and even slight Sb deficiency should
be avoided whenever possible.”
